or_15_2nd_alcove.blurb: A compact sport wall inside Terra Nova, the bolted cliff complex in the Umpqua National Forest hills of southwest Oregon. Around eleven routes, all bolted, start in the 5.8 range and top out in the low 5.12s, though most fall in the 5.10 and 5.11 bracket. Terra Nova climbing tends to be short, steep and bouldery, and many lines begin with a high first bolt, so a stick clip is handy. Holds can be flaky, so wear a helmet. Climbs set back in the alcoves can stay shaded even when the weather is hot, which makes this a decent warm-day pick. Expect a moderate crowd at best.

or_norseman_boulder.blurb: One of several blocks in the Druid Boulders, a bouldering zone hidden in old-growth forest on a hillside below the summit of Marys Peak in Oregon's Coast Range. This block holds about eleven problems, mostly in the easy range: roughly V0 and V1 for most, a couple of V2s, and a single V3. It suits newer boulderers and anyone wanting a mellow forest session. Moss grows fast in this damp climate, so plan on brushing a line or two before you pull on, and dry weather helps a lot. Expect a quiet, shaded setting rather than a crowded crag.

or_harlan_rock_quarry.blurb: A small abandoned quarry in the Siuslaw National Forest, in the Coast Range west of Corvallis and near the old Harlan town site. The wall is sandstone, and the bolted lines sit mostly toward its shorter west end: a spread from easy 5.7 up to 5.11, with one bolted aid line near the middle. Bolts are old, of mixed metals and in poor shape, so treat them with real suspicion. Moisture and vegetation above keep the rock wet or seeping a lot of the time; late spring through fall gives the best chance of dry rock. Quiet, rustic and for the local-crag crowd.

or_troll_s_throne.blurb: A sandstone sub-area on the Callahans ridge west of Roseburg in southwest Oregon. Ten routes, mostly bolted with a trad line and some top-rope options, spanning about 5.7 to 5.11. The bulk sit at 5.9 and 5.10. The style is slabby with a few juggy pulls, a friendly step up for climbers working through the moderate grades. The crag sits under thick conifer forest, so it stays damp for a day or two after rain and collects pine needles and debris that need a brush each spring. A short hike along the ridge trails links it with neighboring walls.

or_hydrotube_area.blurb: The busiest section of Flagstone, an andesite crag in the Willamette National Forest east of Eugene. Ten sport routes run from 5.7 to about 5.11, with the heaviest cluster around 5.9 and 5.10, which is why it draws so many parties looking for good moderates. Several leads are two pitches. The face looks west, so mornings are cool and summer afternoons can turn warm. A brief trail around the base of the rock leads to a tube-shaped feature that marks the spot. Expect company on nice weekends.

or_south_side.blurb: The snow and ice side of Mt. Hood, climbed out of Timberline Lodge by hiking uphill into the eroded crater. The crater is a horseshoe ridge opening southward, from the west rim round to Steel Cliff. About ten routes are listed: mostly short ice and steep-snow lines graded in the lower water-ice range (chiefly WI2 and WI3, with one easier), plus a couple of mountaineering routes including the classic summit line. Conditions swing widely with the season and recent weather, so check before committing. Glacier travel skills and standard alpine gear apply.
